strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem definition: modeling a person's 3D head avatar across a lifelong scale from unstructured photo collections, a direction largely unexplored compared to momentary-level head avatars.

Substantial new resource: TimeWalker-1.0, a large-scale dataset of 40 identities across lifestages (~2.7M frames, diverse age/pose/lighting/ethnicity), with a documented automated construction pipeline, statistics analysis, and a responsible data-use/ethics plan.

Technically coherent framework: the additive neural linear-combination space (canonical average + Neural Head Bases via Dynamo) provides principled handling of sparse per-lifestage data, and Defer-Warping is a sensible solution to dynamic meshing from 2DGS.

Extensive experimental evidence: two evaluation protocols (1-vs-1 and 1-vs-N), comparisons against NeRF-, 3DGS-, generative-, and one-shot-based baselines (including reimplementations where originals are unavailable), ablations on Dynamo, losses, residual embedding, mesh comparisons, cross-identity reenactment on RenderMe-360/INSTA, ID-consistency scoring, and a downstream 3D editing application.

Honest and thorough limitations discussion (large yaw angles, FLAME-driven artifacts, lighting disentanglement imperfections) plus broader-impact analysis including preliminary exploration of combining the framework with large pretrained models.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is moderate: core components (2DGS surfels, INSTA-style inverse warping, FLAME fitting, hashgrid bases) are largely assembled from prior work; the main new elements (Dynamo pruning heuristic, Defer-Warping) are incremental, and Dynamo's threshold-based pruning is heuristic without analysis of sensitivity to kappa/Q or theoretical justification.

Primary quantitative results are confined to 5 selected identities from the authors' own dataset, whose lifestage labels and test splits are constructed by the authors themselves; per-identity variance, significance, and evaluation on more of the 40 identities are not reported in the main paper.

Gains in the 1-vs-N protocol are comparatively modest (PSNR/SSIM roughly on par with single-lifestage Gaussian Surfels models), so the core claim of a unified lifelong space benefits mainly LPIPS; the metric story could be strengthened with geometry or identity metrics across lifestages in the main results.

The framing of a 'disentangled' space is not fully substantiated: the paper itself acknowledges lighting and lifestage entanglement via residual embeddings, and the control dimensions rely on FLAME parameters; disentanglement quality is shown mostly qualitatively.

Comparison fairness is uneven: PAV and GPHM comparisons rely on reimplementations or indirect metric alignment because the originals are not open-sourced, which weakens some claims of superiority over the closest related methods.

Writing and presentation have noticeable issues (typos such as 'propse', inconsistent notation, some duplicated reference entries, e.g., LoRA and NeRF listed twice), and key details (dataset licensing/release status, code availability) remain partially unspecified despite the project-page placeholder.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely new and under-explored problem — lifelong/personalized head avatar modeling from unstructured, cross-age image collections — and provides a clear problem formulation with three well-articulated challenges (long-horizon identity consistency, sparse per-stage data, full-scale controllable animation).

TimeWalker-1.0 is a substantial resource (40 identities, ~2.7M frames spanning ages 20-80, multiple ethnicities, 1024x1024 resolution) that fills a real gap, with a documented construction pipeline, statistics (age/pose/brightness distributions), and a dataset comparison table.

The technical design is coherent: the neural linear-combination space over neural head bases with the Dynamo pruning mechanism is a reasonable extension of classic 3DMM additive principles, and DNA-2DGS with Defer-Warping addresses a practical mesh-sequencing limitation of 2DGS.

The experimental coverage is broad: two comparison protocols (1 vs 1, 1 vs N), comparisons against NeRF-, 3DGS-, generative-, and one-shot-based baselines, external evaluation on the INSTA dataset, ablations on Dynamo, residual embedding, and loss terms, plus downstream applications (reenactment, 3D editing) and honest limitations/ethics discussions.

Cross-protocol results (outperforming multi-model baselines with a single model on PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on both TimeWalker-1.0 and INSTA data) support the claim that shared lifelong representation helps with sparse per-stage data (Table 4 multi- vs single-lifestage).
weaknesses: The evidence for the central 'disentanglement' claim is largely qualitative. There is no quantitative protocol that measures whether lifestage, expression, shape, and appearance axes are truly independent (e.g., expression accuracy on cross-lifestage reenactment, identity metrics across the interpolation of blending weights). Fig. 4/Fig. 11 and the lighting-control discussion (Appendix F.4) even acknowledge imperfect disentanglement, but this is not rigorously quantified in the main paper.

Quantitative gains over the strongest baselines are modest and partly unconvincing. In the 1-vs-N protocol on TimeWalker-1.0, Gaussian-Surfels++ achieves higher PSNR (27.61 vs 27.28); the Dynamo ablation gain is small (27.20 vs 26.94 PSNR, identical LPIPS 0.077); INSTA++ (a self-implemented extension, not the published PAV method) already reaches 26.39. The headline claims rest mostly on LPIPS improvements on the authors' own dataset.

The evaluation protocol is weak: the test set is the last 10% of frames from the same video clips used in training, so PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS primarily measure memorization of near-duplicate frames rather than generalization to unseen expressions, viewpoints, or lifestages — precisely the capabilities the paper claims as contributions. No cross-age or cross-expression held-out evaluation is reported.

Several baselines are not published methods but the authors' own heuristic extensions (INSTA++, Gaussian-Surfels++), while the closest related work (PAV) was not compared directly due to unavailability; comparisons with GPHM are limited to metric alignment through a shared baseline. This weakens the fairness and interpretability of the SOTA claims.

The dataset and its role in the evaluation create a self-referential loop: the method is tuned, ablated, and evaluated almost exclusively on TimeWalker-1.0, and the baselines are adapted by the authors. Only one external dataset (INSTA) is used, and it is not a lifelong dataset (individuals are treated as 'appearances'), which does not validate lifelong modeling per se.

Ethical and legal concerns around the dataset are only partially addressed: 40 celebrities' identities scraped from YouTube/movies without individual consent, used to build animatable lifelike head replicas. The promised non-commercial license and data-use agreement are future commitments; the appropriateness of celebrity data as a public benchmark remains debatable.

Presentation issues undermine confidence: duplicated/confusing table numbering (Table 4/8/9 for ablations), a typo in the conclusion ('propse'), inconsistent citations (GAGAvatar cited as [30] vs [15]), placeholder text ('Project page:'), and key details deferred wholesale to the appendix (training losses, space construction), making the main paper hard to follow as a standalone contribution.

The identity-consistency evaluation (ArcFace score, Table 16) is limited to three identities and compared only against GAGAvatar variants; no user study or perceptual evaluation of the avatar realism, aging plausibility, or animation quality is provided, which is important for a paper whose core value proposition is rendering realism and identity preservation across ages.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely novel and well-motivated problem — lifelong head avatar modeling from unstructured, in-the-wild image collections — which breaks the common 'single-moment identity' assumption of prior avatar work. The framing via the additive combination principle of classic 3DMMs is conceptually clean and well argued.

Two substantive technical components are proposed: (1) the Dynamo module for dynamically pruning/blending neural head bases, with a sensible mechanism (weight-threshold-based hashgrid deactivation) that yields a compact representation; and (2) DNA-2DGS, a reasonable extension of 2DGS to animatable heads combining learned deformation fields with FLAME-driven inverse warping, plus a practical Defer-Warping meshing strategy for dynamic mesh sequences.

The TimeWalker-1.0 dataset (40 identities, 2.7M frames, diverse ages/ethnicities/poses) is a valuable resource contribution that enables the new task, and the paper provides thorough dataset statistics, comparisons to existing datasets, and an honest long-tail analysis.

Experimental evidence is extensive: two evaluation protocols, comparisons against 8+ baselines (NeRF-based, GS-based, generative, one-shot), additional cross-dataset validation on INSTA, identity-consistency scoring via ArcFace, mesh reconstruction comparisons, and multiple ablations (Dynamo, hashgrid counts, residual embedding, losses) that credibly isolate each component's contribution.

The paper is commendably transparent about limitations (large-yaw artifacts, FLAME dependence, data constraints, imperfect lighting disentanglement), includes preliminary studies of large-scale pretrained models, and provides a thoughtful broader-impact and ethics statement with a data-use agreement plan.
weaknesses: Primary quantitative evaluation rests on the authors' own dataset with only 5 selected identities; although cross-validation on INSTA is provided, that experiment reinterprets 9 different individuals as 'appearances' of one person, which is a somewhat artificial proxy for true lifelong variation.

Several key baselines are author-built extensions/re-implementations (INSTA++, Gaussian-Surfels++, PAV re-implementation), and GPHM cannot be compared directly since it is not open-sourced; this leaves some uncertainty about the fairness and optimality of the comparisons that drive the headline claims.

In the more demanding 1-vs-N protocol, the method is not uniformly best (e.g., slightly below Gaussian-Surfels++ in PSNR/SSIM on TimeWalker-1.0); the main advantage is a large LPIPS gap, and no perceptual/user study is included to substantiate the visual realism claims.

The disentanglement of lifestage, lighting, and residual appearance is admitted to be imperfect (artifacts in lighting control, identity drift in some interpolations), which somewhat weakens the 'steerable personalized space' claim; a quantitative disentanglement evaluation is missing.

There is residual clarity risk in the writing (typos such as 'propse', 'Protocal', inconsistent figure/table cross-references, e.g., ablation table numbering), and the core idea — linearly blending per-stage neural features atop a canonical representation — is an incremental composition of known ingredients (hashgrids, 2DGS, INSTA-style warping), so the novelty is primarily in the system design and task definition rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Ethical considerations around building detailed animatable 3D models of real, identifiable celebrities from internet video without their consent are serious; the proposed non-commercial license and access agreement are appropriate but the safeguards remain prospective rather than demonstrated.
